102/// One outgoing data packet on its way to the wire.
103type EgressItem = (DestinationRouting, ApplicationDataOut);
104
105/// The result of asking the PIX egress gate for permission to send one packet.
106///
107/// `Left` is the answer the gate could give synchronously — a permit, or a refusal because the
108/// Session is being torn down. `Right` is the parked case, and the only one that allocates.
109type EgressPermit = futures::future::Either<
110    std::future::Ready<Result<EgressItem, std::io::Error>>,
111    futures::future::BoxFuture<'static, Result<EgressItem, std::io::Error>>,
112>;
113
114/// Passes one outgoing data packet through a Session's PIX egress gate, if it has one.
115///
116/// Returns a future rather than awaiting so this can sit in a `Sink::with` without the combinator
117/// having to box anything in the common case. The gate answers synchronously whenever service is
118/// available — a relaxed load and a compare-exchange — and only the exhausted-budget path allocates,
119/// which is a path that is about to block regardless.
120///
121/// A Session that negotiated no PIX passes through with no gate at all, so an un-supervised Session
122/// pays one `Option` check per packet and nothing else.
123///
124/// Nothing is measured on the admitted arm, deliberately. That arm is the steady state at the
125/// Session's full packet rate, and what an operator wants from it — how much was served, and on
126/// whose money — is already counted inside the gate's own compare-exchange and flushed once per
127/// supervisor turn by [`PixSessionTelemetry`](crate::supervision::telemetry::PixSessionTelemetry).
128/// Only the refused arm, which is about to allocate a boxed future and block, does any telemetry
129/// work of its own.
130///
131/// A packet the gate never admits gives back the SURB its sender counted for it (see
132/// [`count_return_packet_surb`]), since it never reaches the routing resolution that would have taken
133/// one. That covers a packet a closed gate refuses, a park the gate's poisoning fails, and a parked
134/// future dropped with the Session's sink.
135fn acquire_egress_permit(
136    gate: Option<Arc<ServiceGate>>,
137    routing: DestinationRouting,
138    mut data: ApplicationDataOut,
139) -> EgressPermit {
140    let Some(gate) = gate else {
141        return futures::future::Either::Left(std::future::ready(Ok((routing, data))));
142    };
143
144    match gate.try_acquire_sync() {
145        Ok(GateVerdict::Admitted) => futures::future::Either::Left(std::future::ready(Ok((routing, data)))),
146        // Forwarded rather than reconstructed: the gate now names its own error, so both of its
147        // entry points report the same one and neither caller has to know what a refusal means.
148        Err(closed) => {
149            record_gate_closed();
150            data.surb_refund.give_back();
151            futures::future::Either::Left(std::future::ready(Err(std::io::Error::other(closed))))
152        }
153        // Budget exhausted: park until the supervisor funds the front, restores a successor's
154        // allowance, reports front-cycle progress, or gives up on the Session entirely.
155        //
156        // The episode is opened *here*, at the refusal, and moved into the future, so its clock
157        // covers the whole park and its `Drop` closes it however the park ends — resumed, failed,
158        // or cancelled. Opened outside the `async move` rather than inside it because the refusal
159        // has already happened by the time this returns: a future that is constructed and never
160        // polled is still a packet the gate turned away, and starting the clock at first poll
161        // would under-report every stall by however long the caller took to await it.
162        //
163        // One episode per park rather than per refused packet: this sink is serial, so the next
164        // packet is not offered until this future resolves, and a caller cannot open a second
165        // episode by retrying harder.
166        //
167        // The packet's refund is taken off it here and moved in with the episode, for the same
168        // reason: only `Drop` sees every way a park can end without an admission.
169        Ok(GateVerdict::Blocked(reason)) => {
170            let episode = PixGateBlockEpisode::begin(reason);
171            let refund = ParkedSurbRefund(std::mem::take(&mut data.surb_refund));
172            futures::future::Either::Right(Box::pin(async move {
173                let _episode = episode;
174                match gate.acquire().await {
175                    Ok(()) => {
176                        data.surb_refund = refund.admit();
177                        Ok((routing, data))
178                    }
179                    // `refund` gives the SURB back as the future ends.
180                    Err(closed) => Err(std::io::Error::other(closed)),
181                }
182            }))
183        }
184    }
185}

187/// The SURB refund of a packet parked at the PIX egress gate, given back unless the gate admits the
188/// packet.
189///
190/// A park ends without an admission in two ways, and `Drop` sees both: the gate is poisoned, which
191/// fails the park, or the Session's sink is dropped with the parked future in it, polled or not. An
192/// admitted packet takes its refund back with [`admit`](Self::admit), for routing resolution to give
193/// back if the packet starves there.
194struct ParkedSurbRefund(SurbRefund);
195
196impl ParkedSurbRefund {
197    /// The gate admitted the packet: hands its refund back to go on with it.
198    fn admit(mut self) -> SurbRefund {
199        std::mem::take(&mut self.0)
200    }
201}
202
203impl Drop for ParkedSurbRefund {
204    fn drop(&mut self) {
205        // A no-op after `admit`, which leaves an empty refund behind.
206        self.0.give_back();
207    }
208}

210/// How long a teardown waits before retiring its Session's pseudonym from the SURB store's admitted
211/// class.
212///
213/// Derived from the packet pipeline's SURB-resolution window: a return-routed packet whose SURB has
214/// not arrived is retried there for the pipeline's `surb_resolution_wait` — 6 s at the library
215/// default — before it is dropped, and a closing Exit's own notification is exactly such a packet.
216/// The grace must cover the whole wait, so the ring is still there when the resolution stage last
217/// looks; the margin below adds room for the queueing between the send and the lookup, without being
218/// so long that a pseudonym's admitted ring outlives its Session by anything an operator could
219/// notice. The window is operator-configurable, so the grace is derived from it rather than pinned
220/// to a literal that only clears the default.
221fn surb_retire_grace(surb_resolution_wait: Duration) -> Duration {
222    surb_resolution_wait + Duration::from_secs(1)
223}
224
225/// Retires `pseudonym` on behalf of `token`, after a grace derived from the pipeline's
226/// SURB-resolution window (see [`surb_retire_grace`]), when a runtime is running.
227///
228/// Spawned through `Handle::try_current` rather than `tokio::spawn` because the teardowns that
229/// reach this helper are synchronous ([`close_session`], the sessions cache's eviction listener,
230/// [`SessionSlotGuard::drop`]) and can run off-runtime, where `tokio::spawn` panics. The
231/// off-runtime fallback retires inline, which is correct rather than merely convenient: a teardown
232/// with no runtime under it has no packet pipeline resolving return routes on its behalf either, so
233/// the SURB-resolution window the deferral exists to cover cannot be in progress — there is nothing
234/// to wait out.
235fn defer_admission_retire(
236    admission: Option<Arc<dyn SurbAdmissionControl>>,
237    #[cfg_attr(
238        not(any(feature = "runtime-tokio", test, feature = "testing")),
239        allow(unused_variables)
240    )]
241    grace: Duration,
242    session_id: &SessionId,
243    token: AdmissionToken,
244) {
245    let Some(admission) = admission else {
246        return;
247    };
248
249    // The runtime check needs tokio, which this crate carries only behind `runtime-tokio` (and in
250    // test builds). Without it the crate is runtime-agnostic by design, so there is no runtime to
251    // ask for — which is the `Err` branch: retire inline.
252    #[cfg(any(feature = "runtime-tokio", test, feature = "testing"))]
253    match tokio::runtime::Handle::try_current() {
254        Ok(runtime) => {
255            let session_id = *session_id;
256            let retire = async move {
257                tokio::time::sleep(grace).await;
258                tracing::debug!(%session_id, "retiring session pseudonym from the SURB store's admitted class");
259                admission.retire(&session_id, token);
260            };
261            runtime.spawn(retire);
262        }
263        // No runtime: see the doc comment — retire inline, as the synchronous world always did.
264        Err(_) => admission.retire(session_id, token),
265    }
266    #[cfg(not(any(feature = "runtime-tokio", test, feature = "testing")))]
267    admission.retire(session_id, token);
268}

270/// How often a data packet held back for the keep-alive reserve looks at the SURB estimate again.
271const SURB_RESERVE_POLL: Duration = Duration::from_millis(50);
272
273/// SURBs the Exit keeps back from its data, so that its keep-alives can still be sent.
274///
275/// The Exit's SURB-level reports and its distress signals each need a SURB, and nothing else the Exit
276/// sends is as important to the Entry: a report is how a balancer that cannot see the Exit's stock
277/// learns it is running dry. One percent of the Entry's buffer target, at least 32, keeps that many
278/// reports and distress signals sendable: at one report per `surb_balance_notify_period` (15 s in the
279/// node's default configuration) that outlasts minutes of a total outage, long enough for the Entry to
280/// hear it and refill.
281///
282/// Never more than a quarter of the target, as for the PIX fill reserve
283/// ([`effective_surb_reserve`]): an Entry that asks for a buffer shallower than the floor must not
284/// find the Exit unable to send it anything at all.
285fn keep_alive_surb_reserve(target: u64) -> u64 {
286    (target / 100).max(32).min(target / 4)
287}
288
289/// The keep-alive reserve of a Session whose Entry currently asks for the target `balancer` holds.
290///
291/// Read at every check rather than fixed when the Session opens: the Entry may lower its target while
292/// the Session runs (a `BalancerTarget` keep-alive updates it), and its balancer then keeps the stock
293/// near the new one. A reserve fixed at the opening target could sit above every stock the Entry now
294/// keeps, and data would be held for good.
295fn current_keep_alive_surb_reserve(balancer: &BalancerStateValues) -> u64 {
296    keep_alive_surb_reserve(balancer.target_surb_buffer_size.load(Ordering::Relaxed))
297}
298
299/// Holds an outgoing data packet back while the Exit's SURB stock is down to its keep-alive reserve
300/// (see [`current_keep_alive_surb_reserve`]).
301///
302/// Returns `None`, with nothing allocated, in the common case of a stock above the reserve. Otherwise
303/// the future resolves once the stock has risen above it, polling the estimate every
304/// [`SURB_RESERVE_POLL`]. It has no deadline of its own: the Session's own deadlines apply, and a
305/// Session that is closed drops the future with the sink.
306///
307/// Only once the Entry has shown that it refills the stock
308/// ([`BalancerStateValues::counterparty_refills`]): that is, a keep-alive from its balancer, which only an
309/// Entry with a SURB balancer sends (a manual ping, [`KeepAliveFlag::ManualPing`], is not one). An Entry without one
310/// can run a rate-controlled Session too: it announces no target (one that predates this announces the balancer-rate
311/// fallback, which the Exit cannot tell from a real target), attaches one SURB to each data packet and sends no
312/// keep-alives but the odd manual ping. So the announcement says nothing about a balancer either way. A reply held for
313/// a stock above the reserve would then wait until the Entry sent that many more packets.
314///
315/// The Exit's keep-alives do not come through here: its keep-alive stream sends on the message sender
316/// directly (see [`SessionManager::spawn_exit_keep_alive`]), and the PIX fill packets are bounded by
317/// their own `min_surb_reserve`. That is the point of the reserve: they are what it is held for.
318fn hold_for_surb_reserve(
319    session_id: SessionId,
320    estimator: &AtomicSurbFlowEstimator,
321    balancer: &Arc<BalancerStateValues>,
322) -> Option<futures::future::BoxFuture<'static, ()>> {
323    if !balancer.counterparty_refills() {
324        return None;
325    }
326
327    let stock = estimator.saturating_diff();
328    let reserve = current_keep_alive_surb_reserve(balancer);
329    if stock > reserve {
330        return None;
331    }
332
333    debug!(%session_id, stock, reserve, "holding data back: the SURB stock is down to its keep-alive reserve");
334    let (estimator, balancer) = (estimator.clone(), balancer.clone());
335    Some(Box::pin(async move {
336        let held_since = Instant::now();
337        while estimator.saturating_diff() <= current_keep_alive_surb_reserve(&balancer) {
338            hopr_utils::runtime::prelude::sleep(SURB_RESERVE_POLL).await;
339        }
340        tracing::debug!(
341            %session_id,
342            held_for = ?held_since.elapsed(),
343            stock = estimator.saturating_diff(),
344            reserve = current_keep_alive_surb_reserve(&balancer),
345            "releasing held data: the SURB stock is above its keep-alive reserve again"
346        );
347    }))
348}
349
350/// The Exit's data egress for a rate-controlled Session: holds each packet back while the SURB stock
351/// is down to the keep-alive reserve of the target `balancer` holds (once the Entry refills it, see
352/// [`hold_for_surb_reserve`]), books the SURB it consumes, and passes it through the PIX egress gate.
353///
354/// Built as one piece, and not inline where the Session is set up, so that the order of its three
355/// steps can be tested: the SURB is booked only when the packet goes on, so a packet that is held is
356/// not counted against the very stock it is waiting for.
357///
358/// The SURB is booked with the refund that gives it back (see [`count_return_packet_surb`]), as on
359/// every other path a return packet takes: a packet the gate refuses, or one routing resolution drops
360/// for want of a SURB, does not keep the stock the reserve is measured against one low.
361///
362/// `keeps_alive` says whether the Exit runs a keep-alive stream for the Session (a SURB-level
363/// notification period, or PIX fill; see [`SessionManager::spawn_exit_keep_alive`]). The reserve is
364/// kept for that stream, so without one nothing is held back.
365fn exit_data_egress<Si>(
366    sink: Si,
367    session_id: SessionId,
368    estimator: AtomicSurbFlowEstimator,
369    balancer: Arc<BalancerStateValues>,
370    gate: Option<Arc<ServiceGate>>,
371    keeps_alive: bool,
372) -> impl Sink<EgressItem, Error = std::io::Error>
373where
374    Si: Sink<EgressItem, Error = std::io::Error>,
375{
376    sink.with(move |(routing, data): EgressItem| -> EgressPermit {
377        // Each outgoing packet consumes one SURB, given back if the packet never takes it
378        let book_consumed = move |estimator: &AtomicSurbFlowEstimator, data: ApplicationDataOut| {
379            #[cfg(feature = "telemetry")]
380            telemetry::record_session_surb_consumed(&session_id, 1);
381            count_return_packet_surb(estimator, data)
382        };
383        let held = keeps_alive
384            .then(|| hold_for_surb_reserve(session_id, &estimator, &balancer))
385            .flatten();
386        match held {
387            None => acquire_egress_permit(gate.clone(), routing, book_consumed(&estimator, data)),
388            Some(held) => {
389                let (estimator, gate) = (estimator.clone(), gate.clone());
390                futures::future::Either::Right(Box::pin(async move {
391                    held.await;
392                    acquire_egress_permit(gate, routing, book_consumed(&estimator, data)).await
393                }))
394            }
395        }
396    })
397}

399/// Closes an established Session.
400///
401/// Logs the counterpart of "new session established" (see [`SessionSlotGuard::commit`]): one line
402/// per Session at INFO, so its whole lifetime can be read from a production log without the
403/// per-frame detail of the socket.
404///
405/// `admission` is the SURB-store seam, forwarded to [`release_session_slot`]; `None` only ever
406/// reaches here from a teardown that had no seam to call.
407fn close_session(
408    session_id: SessionId,
409    session_data: SessionSlot,
410    reason: ClosureReason,
411    admission: Option<Arc<dyn SurbAdmissionControl>>,
412    grace: Duration,
413    token: AdmissionToken,
414) {
415    tracing::info!(%session_id, %reason, "session closed");
416    release_session_slot(session_id, session_data, reason, admission, grace, token);
417}
418
419/// Tears down a Session slot: stops its tasks and returns what it holds.
420///
421/// Logs nothing at INFO, because it also cleans up a Session whose setup failed before it was
422/// established (see [`SessionSlotGuard`]). An established Session is closed with [`close_session`].
423///
424/// Retires the Session's pseudonym from the SURB store's admitted class, but not immediately: the
425/// retire is pushed past the packet pipeline's SURB-resolution window, so the return-routed
426/// notification a closing Exit has just enqueued — the PIX-failure notice is the one such packet —
427/// still finds its ring when the resolution stage comes to look it up. Retiring inline destroyed
428/// that ring mid-lookup, the packet was dropped, and the Entry never learned that its Session was
429/// gone (hoprnet#8515's `deposit_timeout_closes_session` fails exactly there).
430///
431/// Deferring is only safe because the retire carries the [`AdmissionToken`] its `admit` returned and
432/// the store honours it only while it still names the pseudonym's current admission. Without that
433/// guard, a retire landing in the window could invalidate a *successor* Session's ring: the
434/// pseudonym is client-chosen ([`SessionClientConfig::pseudonym`]) and freely reusable, so a Session
435/// can be re-established on the same one while the previous teardown is still waiting. That failure
436/// is worse than the one being fixed — the successor would go on inserting its SURBs into the small
437/// un-admitted quarantine with nothing logged anywhere — which is why the token is load-bearing here
438/// rather than an optional nicety. Conversely, the guard means no teardown path needs its retire
439/// suppressed: a stale retire is a no-op at the store, never a lost one.
440///
441/// Synchronous-or-spawned, decided by the runtime: when one is running, the delayed retire is spawned
442/// on it; when none is — a `Drop` or the public `close_session` can run off-runtime — the retire
443/// happens inline. The fallback is correct because a teardown with no runtime has no packet pipeline
444/// resolving anything on its behalf either: the SURB-resolution window the deferral exists for is a
445/// property of that pipeline, so there is nothing to wait out, and retiring inline is exactly the
446/// behaviour the synchronous world had before the deferral.
447///
448/// Idempotent by contract, so a rollback — a Session that was never committed, hence never admitted
449/// — pays a no-op here rather than needing a separate "was it admitted?" flag threaded through the
450/// guard.
451///
452/// [`SessionClientConfig::pseudonym`]: crate::SessionClientConfig::pseudonym
453#[tracing::instrument(level = "debug", skip(session_data, admission))]
454fn release_session_slot(
455    session_id: SessionId,
456    session_data: SessionSlot,
457    reason: ClosureReason,
458    admission: Option<Arc<dyn SurbAdmissionControl>>,
459    grace: Duration,
460    token: AdmissionToken,
461) {
462    debug!("closing session");
463
464    // Deferred past the packet pipeline's SURB-resolution window — see the doc comment above — and
465    // made safe by the token, so the retire is never suppressed: a stale one is a no-op at the store.
466    // Cloned rather than moved: the teardown below keeps using `session_id` for the metrics and the
467    // channel bookkeeping that follow the retire.
468    defer_admission_retire(admission, grace, &session_id, token);
469
470    #[cfg(feature = "telemetry")]
471    {
472        set_session_state(&session_id, SessionLifecycleState::Closed);
473        remove_session_metrics_state(&session_id, session_data.pix_egress_gate.get().is_some());
474    }
475
476    if reason != ClosureReason::EmptyRead {
477        // Closing the data sender will also cause it to close from the read side
478        debug!("data tx channel closed on session");
479    }
480
481    // Poison the egress gate before aborting anything. A writer parked on an exhausted predeposit
482    // budget is waiting for a supervisor that is about to stop existing, so it has to be failed
483    // rather than left pending — aborting the tasks first would remove the only thing that could
484    // still have woken it.
485    if let Some(gate) = session_data.pix_egress_gate.get() {
486        gate.poison();
487    }
488
489    // Return this Session's share of the node-level PIX aggregates, after the gate is poisoned so
490    // that no permit it was still handing out is missed. Explicit rather than left to `Drop` for the
491    // reason `CycleBudgetReservation` gives below, and one more: the supervisor worker is spawned
492    // detached and stops only when the last command sender goes with the slot — which the cache does
493    // during a later maintenance pass. Until then the node would report Sessions and cycles that no
494    // longer exist. Idempotent, so the `Drop` backstop is free to run afterwards.
495    if let Some(supervisor) = session_data.pix_supervisor.get() {
496        supervisor.telemetry.release();
497    }
498
499    // Terminate any additional tasks spawned by the Session. This is also what releases the PIX
500    // reconstructor state: the action driver holds a commitment guard per live cycle, and aborting
501    // it drops them.
502    session_data.abort_handles.lock().abort_all();
503
504    // And return the memory those cycles were admitted against, now rather than whenever the last
505    // clone of this slot happens to be dropped. Idempotent, so the slot's own `Drop` — including
506    // the cache's deferred one — is free to run afterwards.
507    if let Some(reservation) = session_data.cycle_budget.as_ref() {
508        reservation.release();
509    }
510
511    #[cfg(all(feature = "telemetry", not(test)))]
512    METRIC_ACTIVE_SESSIONS.decrement(1.0);
513}
514
515/// How a close is answered for a Session whose SURB buffer is already draining.
516///
517/// A `WriteClosed`/`EmptyRead` is the end-of-stream our own ingress abort produces, so it is absorbed
518/// and the drain continues; anything else — a second operator close, or a peer `SessionError` —
519/// overrules the drain by falling through to the hard teardown.
520///
521/// [`begin_surb_drain`](SessionManager::begin_surb_drain) asks it twice, because a Session can be
522/// found draining either before the transition or by losing it to a concurrent close.
523fn answer_while_draining(reason: ClosureReason) -> Option<bool> {
524    matches!(reason, ClosureReason::WriteClosed | ClosureReason::EmptyRead).then_some(true)
525}
526
527fn initiation_timeout_max_one_way(base: Duration, hops: usize) -> Duration {
528    base * (hops as u32)
529}
530
531/// Conservative lower bound on how many coefficient commitments fit into one `SsaCommit` message.
532///
533/// Mirrors the sizing in `SsaClientCommitmentMessage::new_multiple`: payload minus the fixed
534/// prefix (`ssa_index` + `coefficient_index` + `num_polys` + the Start header) and minus a generous
535/// allowance for the CBOR-encoded session id, divided by the per-entry cost
536/// (`PolynomialIndex` + one serialized group element). Using a *lower* bound here means the derived
537/// message count is an over-estimate, which is the safe direction for sizing a queue.
538///
539/// The commitment proof of knowledge is subtracted as well. Every message carries it, since every
540/// message is a constant-term message.
541const MIN_COMMITMENTS_PER_SSA_COMMIT_MSG: usize = {
542    const FIXED_PREFIX: usize = 12;
543    // A `SessionId` is a 10-byte pseudonym; 64 bytes is a large allowance for its CBOR framing.
544    const CBOR_SESSION_ID_ALLOWANCE: usize = 64;
545    const PER_ENTRY: usize = size_of::<hopr_protocol_pix::PolynomialIndex>() + size_of::<HoprPixGroupElement>();
546
547    let usable = ApplicationData::PAYLOAD_SIZE
548        .saturating_sub(FIXED_PREFIX + CBOR_SESSION_ID_ALLOWANCE + HOPR_PIX_COMMITMENT_PROOF_SIZE);
549    let per_msg = usable / PER_ENTRY;
550    if per_msg == 0 { 1 } else { per_msg }
551};
552
553/// Slack added on top of the PIX commitment burst to cover non-PIX Start protocol traffic
554/// (session initiations, establishments, errors, keep-alives).
555const START_PROTOCOL_CHANNEL_RESERVE: usize = 10;
556
557/// Ceiling on the per-session term of [`start_protocol_channel_capacity`].
558///
559/// A session contributes to this channel only while its Start exchange is in flight — a handful of
560/// messages between initiation and establishment — after which it is silent apart from PIX, which
561/// the commitment term already covers. So the queue depth tracks concurrent *handshakes*, not the
562/// total number of sessions the node may manage, and `maximum_managed_sessions` (validated up to
563/// 100 000) is the wrong quantity to size a pre-allocated ring from.
564const MAX_CONCURRENT_START_EXCHANGES: usize = 10_000;
565
566/// Capacity of the Start protocol ingress channel.
567///
568/// This channel is fed by [`SessionManager::dispatch_message`] with `try_send`, and an overflow
569/// **drops** the message. For most Start messages that is recoverable, but a dropped `SsaCommit`
570/// is not: there is no NACK or retransmission, so the corresponding coefficient cell stays empty
571/// forever, the commitment never completes, every subsequent share fails to verify, and the cycle
572/// dies on the supervisor's `max_deposit_wait` deadline.
573///
574/// PIX changed this channel's load from roughly one message per session to the *entire* commitment
575/// set of an SSA cycle, chunked into packet-sized messages, plus a reserve for ordinary Start
576/// traffic. Batching multiplies that: an Exit may ask for up to
577/// [`ssas_per_request`](crate::SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request) SSAs at once and gets that many
578/// cycles' commitment sets back-to-back, all landing here, so the per-cycle term is scaled by the
579/// configured maximum even when dynamic admission selects less for a particular Session.
580///
581/// The per-cycle burst is bounded by two independent limits, and the capacity takes the smaller:
582///
583/// * `quota_range.end() / PIX_QUOTA_BYTES_PER_SHARE` is `polys × (threshold + surplus)`, an over-estimate by that whole
584///   second factor, since a cycle carries one constant term per polynomial and nothing else. The quota alone does not
585///   reveal how the product splits, so the over-estimate cannot be undone from it.
586/// * [`MAX_POLYS_PER_SSA`] is the number of polynomials [`SessionManager::check_pix_params`] will accept, whatever the
587///   quota says. It therefore bounds the commitments a cycle can ever deliver.
588///
589/// Clamping to the second matters because this capacity is *reserved*, not merely enforced:
590/// `crossfire`'s array flavour pre-allocates every slot when the channel is built. An
591/// operator-settable `quota_range` feeding an unclamped derivation is an allocation with no upper
592/// bound — at `quota_range.end() = 1e13` it asks for 77 GB. Over-provisioning is still the safe
593/// direction within the clamp, and the surviving margin is large: the default dimensions burst
594/// ≈ 160 messages against a capacity term of ≈ 648.
595///
596/// The batch factor is bounded by [`MAX_SSA_BATCH_SIZE`] for the same allocation reason, and is
597/// clamped here rather than being taken on trust from the config, so that callers which build a
598/// `SessionManagerConfig` without going through [`SessionManager::new`] cannot inflate it.
599///
600/// The session term is clamped for the same reason. `maximum_managed_sessions` validates up to
601/// 100 000, and one slot holds a `(HoprPseudonym, HoprStartProtocol)` sized by the enum's largest
602/// variant, so an operator raising the session limit would silently buy a multi-megabyte startup
603/// allocation. Ordinary Start traffic is one message per session *in flight*, not one per session
604/// the node will ever manage, so [`MAX_CONCURRENT_START_EXCHANGES`] is the honest bound.
605fn start_protocol_channel_capacity(cfg: &SessionManagerConfig) -> usize {
606    let max_commitments = (*cfg.pix_config.quota_range.end() / PIX_QUOTA_BYTES_PER_SHARE).min(MAX_POLYS_PER_SSA as u64);
607    let max_commit_msgs = max_commitments.div_ceil(MIN_COMMITMENTS_PER_SSA_COMMIT_MSG as u64);
608    let ssas_per_request = cfg.pix_config.supervision.ssas_per_request.clamp(1, MAX_SSA_BATCH_SIZE) as u64;
609
610    // `usize::try_from` cannot fail on 64-bit targets; saturate rather than panic on 32-bit ones.
611    usize::try_from(max_commit_msgs.saturating_mul(ssas_per_request))
612        .unwrap_or(usize::MAX)
613        .saturating_add(cfg.maximum_sessions.min(MAX_CONCURRENT_START_EXCHANGES))
614        .saturating_add(START_PROTOCOL_CHANNEL_RESERVE)
615}

617/// Minimum time the SURB buffer must endure if no SURBs are being produced.
618pub const MIN_SURB_BUFFER_DURATION: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1);
619/// Minimum time between SURB buffer notifications to the Entry.
620pub const MIN_SURB_BUFFER_NOTIFICATION_PERIOD: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1);
621
622/// Fastest return-path rate a Session is assumed to sustain, in packets per second.
623///
624/// Bounds the PIX `max_recovery_time` from below: a deadline this rate cannot meet is treated as one
625/// no Session can, so without fill it is the floor itself, and with fill it caps the `fill.max_rate`
626/// the floor may count on. Stated in packets, because per-packet work is what limits a Session, so it does not
627/// move with any packet or segment size; it carries ≈ 58 Mbps of Session data at full
628/// [`SESSION_MTU`] segments.
629pub const MAX_ASSUMED_SESSION_PACKET_RATE: u64 = 5000;
630
631/// The first challenge value used in Start protocol to initiate a session.
632pub(crate) const MIN_CHALLENGE: StartChallenge = 1;
633
634/// Maximum time to wait for counterparty to receive the target number of SURBs.
635const SESSION_READINESS_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10);
636
637/// How long the Entry holds a *near-miss* `SsaRequest` while the Exit's returned data catches up to
638/// the successor boundary.
639///
640/// Absorbs mixer reordering between the returned packets and the `SsaRequest` they earned — the two
641/// travel the same mixed path, so the request can arrive ahead of the last few packets that
642/// justified it. Nothing longer: a sustained shortfall never reaches this wait, because the gate only
643/// enters it for a request already within one emission window of the boundary.
644///
645/// Comfortably inside the Exit's `max_ssa_delivery_time` (20 s by default, batch-scaled), which is
646/// what closes the Session as `CommitmentTimeout` if no `SsaCommit` follows. That budget also has to
647/// cover generating the commitments and shipping the burst, so this takes a small slice of it.
648const SSA_SUCCESSOR_SERVICE_WAIT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2);
649
650/// How often [`SSA_SUCCESSOR_SERVICE_WAIT`] re-reads the returned-packet count.
651///
652/// Polled rather than notified: the alternative is waking a waiter from the Session receive path,
653/// which would put a branch on every inbound packet to serve a case that arises once per SSA cycle.
654const SSA_SUCCESSOR_SERVICE_POLL: Duration = Duration::from_millis(250);
655
656/// How long after a batch's commitments last went out the Entry takes a repeat of its request to
657/// mean that they were lost on the way, rather than that the repeat crossed them.
658///
659/// The Exit repeats a successor request while some member of it has received no part of its
660/// commitment. A repeat it sent before the burst reached it can still be arriving up to a round trip
661/// after the burst went out, and answering that one would spend a retransmission on a burst that is
662/// not lost. A repeat that arrives later says the burst went out and none of it arrived. Publishing
663/// a burst only means the local transport took it, and a relayer that dies on the forward path loses
664/// all of it. The Exit then has no part it could name in a scoped re-request, so the repeat is the
665/// only prompt there is. See [`SessionSsaState::unpublished`].
666///
667/// Well over a round trip, and equal to the Exit's default re-send interval. A path slower than this
668/// costs at most one needless re-send per grace, and each re-send spends one of the cycle's
669/// [`MAX_COMMITMENT_RETRANSMISSIONS`](hopr_protocol_pix::MAX_COMMITMENT_RETRANSMISSIONS).
670const SSA_REPEAT_RESEND_GRACE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(3);
671
672/// Standard deviations below an honest Exit's expected returned packets at which the successor gate
673/// sets its bar — see [`successor_required_packets`].
674///
675/// Four put the chance that an Exit losing exactly the tolerated share fraction falls short of the
676/// bar at 3 × 10⁻⁵, and that it falls short by more than the near-miss window — refused without
677/// waiting — at about one in 1.5 million at the deployed split (normal approximation). A shortfall
678/// inside the window still gets [`SSA_SUCCESSOR_SERVICE_WAIT`] for the Session's ongoing traffic to
679/// make it up. The price is ~0.33 % of the boundary added to what an Exit can withhold and still be
680/// funded: the deployed bar moves from 41.3 % of a cycle's packets to 41.0 %.
681const SUCCESSOR_GATE_ARRIVAL_SIGMAS: f64 = 4.0;
682
683/// Returned packets the successor gate demands of an Exit whose boundary is `target` packets, at the
684/// share loss `tolerated_loss` the negotiated split survives.
685///
686/// `floor(max(0, μ − zσ))` for an Exit's arrivals at exactly that loss, `Binomial(target, 1 − L)`:
687/// `μ = target · (1 − L)`, `σ = √(target · L · (1 − L))` and `z` [`SUCCESSOR_GATE_ARRIVAL_SIGMAS`].
688/// A split with no surplus tolerates no loss, so σ is zero and the whole target is demanded exactly.
689///
690/// A tolerance near one floors at one packet, not zero, for any non-zero target: the bound is at most
691/// `μ ≤ target`, so one is never more than the boundary itself. Without it a tiny boundary under a
692/// huge surplus (`128 × (2 + 255)`: μ 10.8, σ 3.2) demands nothing, the near-miss wait never starts
693/// on zero returned packets, and the successor is funded on the Entry's own emission alone. An Exit
694/// that has returned nothing since its first commitment has shown no service whatever split the Entry
695/// chose. The cost is an honest Exit at the tolerated loss returning nothing with probability
696/// `L^target` — 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ at `128 × (2 + 255)`, the order of the 4σ bound's own 3 × 10⁻⁵ — and
697/// it bites only at degenerate cycles of a few dozen packets (`8 × (2 + 255)`: 0.59), where no
698/// statistic means anything.
699///
700/// An `f64` carries both terms to well under a packet below a watermark of 10⁹ cycles.
701fn successor_required_packets(target: u64, tolerated_loss: f64) -> u64 {
702    let bar_floor = target.min(1);
703    let target = target as f64;
704    let delivered = 1.0 - tolerated_loss;
705    let mean = target * delivered;
706    let deviation = (target * tolerated_loss * delivered).sqrt();
707    // The cast floors, the clamped bound being non-negative.
708    let bound = (mean - SUCCESSOR_GATE_ARRIVAL_SIGMAS * deviation).max(0.0) as u64;
709    bound.max(bar_floor)
710}
711
712/// Minimum timeout until an unfinished frame is discarded.
713const MIN_FRAME_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_millis(10);
714
715/// Hard ceiling on both SSA batch-size knobs, whatever the configuration says.
716///
717/// The current maximum value of 9 is based on the current available pool limitations.
718///
719/// Deliberately far below the wire limit (`StartProtocol::MAX_SSAS_PER_REQUEST`, 27), which only
720/// bounds what can be *decoded*. The real cost is paid on both sides of the exchange and neither is
721/// small at the profiled dimensions:
722///
723/// * Entry: every entry in the batch is a full `new_ssa_commitment` (hundreds of thousands of EC commitments), its own
724///   burst of thousands of `SsaCommit` packets, and its own `ReadyToDeposit` — i.e. its own on-chain deposit.
725/// * Exit: every entry is a live reconstructor cycle, held until that cycle recovers — worst case ≈15.4 MiB at the
726///   deployed dimensions (`hopr_protocol_pix::peak_cycle_bytes`), so ≈138 MiB per Session at this ceiling, before the
727///   pipelining factor. That is what a Session reserves against [`IncomingSessionPixConfig::max_live_cycle_bytes`], so
728///   raising the batch size directly divides how many PIX Sessions the node will accept.
729///
730/// It also bounds the supervisor's deadline scaling: a batch multiplies both
731/// [`max_ssa_delivery_time`](crate::SupervisorConfig::max_ssa_delivery_time) and
732/// [`max_deposit_wait`](crate::SupervisorConfig::max_deposit_wait), and that product is what decides
733/// how long a Session may be served unincentivized.
734///
735/// Both [`SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request`](crate::SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request) and
736/// [`SessionManagerConfig::max_ssas_per_ssa_request`] are clamped to `1..=Self` where they are read,
737/// so a programmatically built config that never calls `validate()` cannot exceed it.
738pub const MAX_SSA_BATCH_SIZE: usize = 9;
739
740// The Entry's retention of commitment material has to outlast the batch that material belongs to.
741// `hopr-protocol-pix` cannot see this figure, so it derives its cap from it in prose; this is the
742// half of that derivation which has to hold. A cycle must stay retransmittable at least until its
743// own batch has finished being committed, or a commitment packet lost early in a large batch becomes
744// unrepairable while the rest of the batch is still arriving. Slack beyond one batch is a judgement
745// call, which is why this is an inequality and not the equality the two figures satisfy today.
746const _: () = assert!(
747    hopr_protocol_pix::MAX_RETAINED_COMMITMENT_CYCLES >= MAX_SSA_BATCH_SIZE,
748    "MAX_SSA_BATCH_SIZE exceeds MAX_RETAINED_COMMITMENT_CYCLES, so a cycle can be evicted from the Entry's retention \
749     before its own batch is fully committed and its commitment stops being repairable"
750);
751
752/// How long an Exit waits for the deposit pool to answer a
753/// [`DepositDataRequest`](HoprSessionOutPixEvent::DepositDataRequest) before sending the batch
754/// without what has not arrived.
755pub const DEPOSIT_DATA_REQUEST_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(3);
756
757/// SSA batches whose reconstructor state can be live on the Exit at the same moment.
758///
759/// Two, enforced at allocation rather than inferred from share-order policy. The supervisor tags
760/// every requested generation and defers a successor while this many generations still own live
761/// reconstructor state; it also checks the equivalent full-batch cycle count charged below. Full
762/// recovery releases cycle state immediately, after which a deferred request is retried.
763///
764/// Used as the pipelining factor when a Session reserves against
765/// [`IncomingSessionPixConfig::max_live_cycle_bytes`].
766pub const MAX_OVERLAPPING_BATCHES: u64 = 2;
767
768/// What a PIX Session at these dimensions costs the node's live-cycle budget.
769///
770/// The worst case one cycle can hold, times every cycle that can be live at once. Both factors come
771/// from configuration rather than observation, because the charge is made before the Session exists.
772/// `ssas_per_request` is clamped for the reason [`SessionManager::new`] clamps it — a
773/// programmatically built config must not be able to understate the reservation and then overrun it.
774pub fn cycle_budget_for(params: &PixParams, ssas_per_request: usize) -> u64 {
775    hopr_protocol_pix::peak_cycle_bytes::<HoprPixSpec>(params)
776        .saturating_mul(ssas_per_request.clamp(1, MAX_SSA_BATCH_SIZE) as u64)
777        .saturating_mul(MAX_OVERLAPPING_BATCHES)
778}
779
780/// The largest reservation any offer inside a `quota_range` ending at `quota_bytes` can produce.
781///
782/// The quota fixes `polys × (threshold + surplus)` but not the split, and the two terms of
783/// [`hopr_protocol_pix::peak_cycle_bytes`] pull opposite ways — the share buffers want a high
784/// threshold, the per-polynomial overhead wants many polynomials — so the maximum is found by
785/// walking the thresholds rather than by a closed form. 254 iterations, once, at config load.
786///
787/// `surplus = 0` throughout, which is what makes each candidate the worst of its threshold: the
788/// surplus is priced into the quota but holds no reconstructor state, so any surplus at all buys
789/// fewer polynomials for the same quota.
790///
791/// Used to reject a [`IncomingSessionPixConfig::max_live_cycle_bytes`] that could never admit even
792/// one Session at the dimensions its own `quota_range` advertises.
793pub fn max_cycle_budget_for_quota(quota_bytes: u64, ssas_per_request: usize) -> u64 {
794    let quota_shares = quota_bytes / PIX_QUOTA_BYTES_PER_SHARE;
795
796    (hopr_protocol_pix::MIN_POLY_THRESHOLD..=hopr_protocol_pix::MAX_POLY_THRESHOLD)
797        .filter_map(|threshold| {
798            let polys = u16::try_from((quota_shares / threshold as u64).min(MAX_POLYS_PER_SSA as u64)).ok()?;
799            PixParams::try_new(polys, threshold, 0, LOCAL_PIX_SUITE).ok()
800        })
801        .map(|params| cycle_budget_for(&params, ssas_per_request))
802        .max()
803        .unwrap_or_default()
804}

806/// Default for [`SessionManagerConfig::max_ssas_per_ssa_request`] — how many SSA commitments an Entry
807/// accepts in a single [`SsaServerCommitmentMessage`].
808///
809/// Pipelining needs at most one cycle in flight ahead of the active one, so 2 leaves room for an Exit
810/// batching at the default without turning one inbound packet into an unbounded amount of Entry work
811/// and on-chain deposits.
812pub const DEFAULT_MAX_SSAS_PER_SSA_REQUEST: usize = 2;
813
814/// Default for [`SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request`](crate::SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request) —
815/// how many SSAs an Exit may ask for in a single [`SsaServerCommitmentMessage`]. It is the maximum
816/// in dynamic mode and the exact batch in fixed mode.
817///
818/// One, so that the default configuration produces exactly the unbatched exchange: same wire bytes,
819/// same supervisor deadlines, same Start protocol channel capacity.
820pub const DEFAULT_SSAS_PER_SSA_REQUEST: usize = 1;

822/// Timeout when sending Start protocol messages to the sink
823const EXTERNAL_SEND_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_millis(200);
824
825// Needs to use an UnboundedSender instead of oneshot
826// because Moka cache requires the value to be Clone, which oneshot Sender is not.
827// It also cannot be enclosed in an Arc, since calling `send` consumes the oneshot Sender.
828// The Session initiation cache is only present on the Entry (client) side.
829type SessionInitiationCache = moka::sync::Cache<
830    StartChallenge,
831    crossfire::MTx<crossfire::mpsc::One<Result<StartEstablished<SessionId>, StartErrorType<SessionId>>>>,
832>;
833
834/// Handles to streams and tasks spawned by the Session.
835#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
836enum SessionHandles {
837    /// Handle to the stream that facilitates ingress of data from the HOPR network into the Session.
838    Ingress,
839    /// Handle to the process that sends keep-alive messages to the Session recipient (Exit).
840    KeepAlive,
841    /// Handle to the one-shot timer that turns the SURB-level notification on after its first period.
842    ///
843    /// Registered rather than fired and forgotten: it holds an `Arc<PixFillControl>` for as long as
844    /// the period lasts, and no maximum is enforced on that period, so an unregistered task keeps a
845    /// closed Session's fill control alive for however long the operator configured.
846    SurbNotifyDelay,
847    /// Handle to the process that monitors and balances SURBs.
848    Balancer,
849    /// Handle to the task that executes the PIX supervisor's actions.
850    ///
851    /// One per Session rather than one per cycle: the supervisor multiplexes every SSA it tracks
852    /// onto a single action stream.
853    PixActionDriver,
854    /// Handle to the process that awaits the PIX deposit for one SSA.
855    ///
856    /// Carries the inner `SsaIndex` value so that each cycle's observer is independent — pipelining
857    /// must not cancel an earlier cycle's.
858    PixDepositObserver(u32),
859}
860
861impl std::fmt::Display for SessionHandles {
862    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
863        match self {
864            Self::Ingress => write!(f, "Ingress"),
865            Self::KeepAlive => write!(f, "KeepAlive"),
866            Self::SurbNotifyDelay => write!(f, "SurbNotifyDelay"),
867            Self::Balancer => write!(f, "Balancer"),
868            Self::PixActionDriver => write!(f, "PixActionDriver"),
869            Self::PixDepositObserver(idx) => write!(f, "PixDepositObserver({idx})"),
870        }
871    }
872}
873
874/// The PIX dimensions this Session negotiated, on the Exit side.
875///
876/// Once carried the SSA index and a fault counter as well. Both moved to the supervisor: it decides
877/// *when* a cycle is requested, so it is also what allocates the index, and it is what enforces the
878/// fault limit. Leaving a second copy of either here would have meant two authorities for one fact.
879#[derive(Debug)]
880struct SessionSsaState {
881    /// The dimensions this Session negotiated, as they went on the wire.
882    params: PixParams,
883    /// Highest SSA index this Session has had the generator commit to, `0` before the first batch.
884    ///
885    /// A deliberate second copy of a fact the generator already holds, and the only one of the three
886    /// that came back. The generator's own watermark lives in a cache with an idle retention, so
887    /// "absent" there conflates *never committed* with *state discarded* — and those must not be
888    /// treated alike, because the first is the opening batch every Session begins with and the second
889    /// is a Session whose Entry can no longer serve the cycles it already committed to. This copy
890    /// lives exactly as long as the Session does, so it can tell them apart. See the successor gate in
891    /// [`SessionManager::handle_ssa_request`].
892    ///
893    /// Entry-side only; an Exit never commits and leaves it at zero. [`SsaIndex`] is a `NonZero<u32>`,
894    /// which is what makes `0` an unambiguous "none" rather than a sentinel that has to be defended.
895    committed_ssa_watermark: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU32,
896    /// [`SessionSlot::returned_packets`] as it stood when this Session first committed.
897    ///
898    /// The successor gate counts service *since* that instant, not since the Session opened. Before
899    /// the first commitment the generator holds no polynomials, so the SURBs going out carry no
900    /// shares — and an Exit may legitimately be served up to `max_predeposit_packets` of them before
901    /// any deposit exists. Crediting that prefix would let the Exit bank unpaid service against the
902    /// first cycle it *is* paid for. Everything after this point rides a share.
903    returned_at_first_commit: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU64,
904    /// Lowest SSA index of the request this Session most recently committed to, `0` before the first.
905    ///
906    /// What lets the Entry tell a *repeat* of a request it already served from a *stale* one. Both
907    /// ask for an index at or below [`committed_ssa_watermark`](Self::committed_ssa_watermark); only
908    /// a repeat names the batch that was last committed. The Exit re-sends an unanswered successor
909    /// request until it hears back, so a repeat is the ordinary case once a request is admitted and
910    /// the first burst is still on its way, and answering it with a second commitment would fund the
911    /// same cycle twice.
912    ///
913    /// Stored once phase two has staged the whole request rather than after the burst is published.
914    /// A burst that fails to send has still moved the generator, so its re-sends must read as repeats —
915    /// read as stale instead, each of them would be logged as a fault. Not stored any earlier, though:
916    /// a batch that fails *during* phase two after moving the generator can never be committed, and
917    /// that failure closes the Session rather than leaving its re-sends to be told apart. And a repeat
918    /// is not always a no-op: while [`unpublished`](Self::unpublished) still holds members of that
919    /// batch, the repeat is the Exit's prompt to finish publishing them, and once it has been published
920    /// a repeat that comes too late to have crossed the bursts is the prompt to send them again.
921    last_committed_first: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU32,
922    /// Members of the batch last staged whose commitment burst and `ReadyToDeposit` have not both gone
923    /// out, with exactly the announcement that is still owed for each.
924    ///
925    /// Phase three sends a member's whole burst and only then announces its deposit address, and the
926    /// transport can fail between any two messages (it gives up on a send after
927    /// [`EXTERNAL_SEND_TIMEOUT`]). Without this record the generator has moved on and the failure is
928    /// final: the Exit's re-sends read as repeats of a batch the Entry believes it served, and a
929    /// scoped re-request completes the commitment it names without ever announcing the deposit, so the
930    /// Exit holds a complete commitment for a cycle nobody was told to fund.
931    ///
932    /// Filled at the end of phase two for every staged member, before anything is sent. **A member is
933    /// published by whoever removes it from here, under this mutex**, and by nobody else: phase three
934    /// claims each member just before its burst, and the resumption that finishes an interrupted batch
935    /// ([`resume_publication`]) claims the same way. Whoever holds the claim announces the deposit once
936    /// its whole burst is out, so the announcement happens at most once per member however many
937    /// resumers there are — which matters, because the scoped re-request path does not take the
938    /// per-pseudonym request lock. A claimant that fails puts its member back, and a member that was
939    /// never claimed was never touched.
940    ///
941    /// A newer batch replaces whatever is left of an older one: the Exit asks for a successor only
942    /// after the commitment and the deposit of its predecessor, so an older member still here has been
943    /// given up on. That, and the batch size the Entry accepts, bound the map. A claimant of an older
944    /// batch that fails after it was replaced finds its member not wanted back (see [`OwedPublications`]).
945    ///
946    /// **What this recovers, and what it does not.** Only the Exit can prompt a resumption: by a repeat
947    /// of the request, or by a scoped re-request that names an owed cycle. The Exit re-requests the
948    /// parts of a commitment that has started to arrive and gone quiet, so a member cut part-way
949    /// through its burst is finished by the re-request wherever its batch stands — and that resumption
950    /// publishes every member still owed, not only the one named. A member with *no message of it out*
951    /// has nothing to re-request, and only a repeat can reach it. The Exit repeats a successor batch,
952    /// whole, for as long as any member of it has reported nothing, **but only while the batch is behind
953    /// the front**: a batch at the front is never re-sent (the opening batch is at the front from the
954    /// start, and a successor admitted just before the front moved joins it). So, per member, nothing
955    /// prompts a resumption in two cases, and a third is given up on:
956    ///
957    /// * a member with no message of it out whose batch holds the front: the opening batch always, or any member after
958    ///   a cut that lands exactly on a member boundary there, when no earlier member of the batch is itself still owed
959    ///   (its own burst cut part-way), whose re-request would resume it too. The member times out on its commitment
960    ///   deadline;
961    /// * a burst that went out whole whose `ReadyToDeposit` could not be queued because the PIX event channel was
962    ///   full. The Exit then holds a complete commitment and never asks again. The member is kept owed, in case
963    ///   something does;
964    /// * a cycle whose retransmissions are spent, which can never be published again. It is dropped from here with one
965    ///   warning (see [`resume_publication`]).
966    ///
967    /// A member that has been published is out of the owed set, but publishing only means the local
968    /// transport took the burst. If a relayer on the forward path dies, the whole burst can still be
969    /// lost. The Exit then has no part it could re-request, so only a repeat reaches the member. A
970    /// repeat that arrives more than [`SSA_REPEAT_RESEND_GRACE`] after the batch last went out has the
971    /// whole burst of every announced member sent again, and nothing announced (see
972    /// [`OwedPublications::announced`]). The limits are the same as for a resumption: a batch at the
973    /// front is never repeated, so a lost opening burst is not recovered, and each re-send spends one
974    /// of the cycle's retransmissions.
975    ///
976    /// None of these strands a deposit, because nothing was announced for the member concerned: the
977    /// Exit's own deadline ends the cycle. The opposite hazard exists, though. A resumed burst answers a
978    /// re-request, and the Exit's re-request timer asks until just before the cycle's commitment
979    /// deadline without moving it, so the resumption — or a repeat delayed on the way — can arrive after
980    /// the Exit has retired the cycle. A re-send is a second source of the same thing: re-sends go on
981    /// up to the deadline of a member that has reported a part, which the tick does not push, so the
982    /// last one — sent up to one interval before the Exit retires that member — can resume and announce
983    /// it afterwards. The Entry then announces a deposit for an address nobody can reconstruct.
984    unpublished: parking_lot::Mutex<OwedPublications>,
985    /// The refusal this Session last logged, as `(lowest index asked for, SsaRefusal)`, `0` for none.
986    ///
987    /// Only to keep the log honest. The Exit re-sends a refused request every few seconds, so the
988    /// same refusal repeats for as long as the gate stays shut, and a line per re-send would bury the
989    /// one that matters: the first.
990    last_refusal: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU64,
991    /// What this Exit sent as deposit data, per SSA index, for cycles whose deposit address it has
992    /// not learned yet.
993    sent_deposit_data: Arc<parking_lot::Mutex<HashMap<SsaIndex, HoprPixDepositPayload>>>,
994}
995
996/// The members of the batch last staged that are still owed their publication, and the ones that
997/// have had it.
998///
999/// The members are what is owed; the `batch` counter is there for one reason. A member that was
1000/// claimed is out of the map while its publication is attempted, and if that attempt fails it is put
1001/// back — but not if a newer batch has been staged meanwhile, whose members have replaced the older
1002/// ones. Which batch a returning member belongs to cannot be read off its index, since a member
1003/// returning to its own batch can sit below the ones still in the map just as an old one does, so each
1004/// staging gets a number and each claim carries it.
1005#[derive(Debug, Default)]
1006struct OwedPublications {
1007    /// Which staging the members belong to. Incremented every time a batch is staged.
1008    batch: u64,
1009    members: BTreeMap<SsaIndex, AgreedSsaQuota>,
1010    /// Members of the same batch whose publication completed: their whole burst went out and their
1011    /// `ReadyToDeposit` was queued.
1012    ///
1013    /// The only members a late repeat may have sent again
1014    /// ([`SessionSsaState::claim_republication`]). Sending the burst of a member that is owed, or
1015    /// that someone is publishing right now, would hand the Exit a complete commitment for a cycle
1016    /// nobody has yet been told to fund.
1017    announced: BTreeSet<SsaIndex>,
1018    /// When a burst of this batch last went out in full, `None` before the first.
1019    last_sent: Option<Instant>,
1020}
1021
1022/// A member taken out of [`OwedPublications`] by whoever is publishing it.
1023///
1024/// Holding one is the right to publish the member and announce its deposit. It is either spent by
1025/// completing the publication ([`SessionSsaState::complete_publication`]) or handed back to
1026/// [`SessionSsaState::restore_unpublished`].
1027#[derive(Debug)]
1028struct ClaimedPublication {
1029    /// The staging the member was claimed from.
1030    batch: u64,
1031    /// What `ReadyToDeposit` is to say once the member's burst is out.
1032    quota: AgreedSsaQuota,
1033}
1034
1035/// Why `handle_ssa_request` dropped a request without committing to it, short of refusing the Session.
1036///
1037/// Part of the key `SessionSsaState::note_refusal` deduplicates the log on, and the discriminant is
1038/// what goes into it, so the values are never `0`.
1039#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
1040enum SsaRefusal {
1041    /// The batch committed up to now has not been emitted far enough for any conforming Exit to ask.
1042    Early = 1,
1043    /// Emission is far enough, but the packets that came back are fewer than the batch has earned.
1044    /// Expected on a multi-hop path, where the Entry sees the packets that survive the whole return
1045    /// path and the Exit counts the ones its first relayer acknowledged.
1046    UnderServed = 2,
1047    /// The request names indices at or below what was committed, and not the batch committed last.
1048    Stale = 3,
1049}
1050
1051impl SsaRefusal {
1052    /// Logs one refusal at the level its kind and novelty call for.
1053    ///
1054    /// An under-served request is the expected way a transient shortfall looks, so its first
1055    /// occurrence is information; an early one comes from an Exit that is not conforming, and a stale
1056    /// one from an Exit that has lost track of the Session, so theirs are warnings. Every repeat is a
1057    /// debug line — the first already said it.
1058    fn log(self, first_time: bool, session_id: &SessionId, error: &SessionManagerError) {
1059        let what = match self {
1060            Self::Early => "refused an early SSA request",
1061            Self::UnderServed => "refused an under-served SSA request",
1062            Self::Stale => "refused a stale SSA request",
1063        };
1064        match (first_time, self) {
1065            (false, _) => tracing::debug!(%session_id, %error, "{what} (repeated)"),
1066            (true, Self::UnderServed) => tracing::info!(%session_id, %error, "{what}"),
1067            (true, Self::Early | Self::Stale) => tracing::warn!(%session_id, %error, "{what}"),
1068        }
1069    }
1070}
1071
1072impl SessionSsaState {
1073    pub fn new(params: PixParams) -> Self {
1074        Self {
1075            params,
1076            committed_ssa_watermark: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU32::new(0),
1077            returned_at_first_commit: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU64::new(0),
1078            last_committed_first: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU32::new(0),
1079            unpublished: Default::default(),
1080            last_refusal: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU64::new(0),
1081            sent_deposit_data: Default::default(),
1082        }
1083    }
1084
1085    /// Files the deposit data of a batch the Exit is about to send, for
1086    /// [`take_sent_deposit_data`](Self::take_sent_deposit_data) to hand back once the matching
1087    /// deposit address is known.
1088    pub fn remember_sent_deposit_data(&self, deposit_data: &HashMap<SsaIndex, HoprPixDepositPayload>) {
1089        let mut sent = self.sent_deposit_data.lock();
1090        for (&ssa_index, payload) in deposit_data {
1091            sent.insert(ssa_index, payload.clone());
1092        }
1093    }
1094
1095    /// Removes and returns what this Exit sent for `ssa_index`, or empty data if it sent none.
1096    pub fn take_sent_deposit_data(&self, session_id: &SessionId, ssa_index: SsaIndex) -> PixDepositData {
1097        PixDepositData {
1098            id: PixAddressId::new(session_id, ssa_index),
1099            data: self
1100                .sent_deposit_data
1101                .lock()
1102                .remove(&ssa_index)
1103                .map(|payload| payload.0)
1104                .unwrap_or_default(),
1105        }
1106    }
1107
1108    /// Highest SSA index committed for this Session, `None` before the first batch.
1109    #[inline]
1110    pub fn committed_watermark(&self) -> Option<SsaIndex> {
1111        SsaIndex::new(self.committed_ssa_watermark.load(Ordering::Relaxed))
1112    }
1113
1114    /// Raises the committed-index watermark to `index` if it is higher, taking the returned-packet
1115    /// baseline on the first commitment.
1116    ///
1117    /// `fetch_max` rather than a store: the gate serialises requests per pseudonym, but a Session's
1118    /// slot is shared and monotonicity here must not depend on that lock staying where it is. Its
1119    /// *previous* value is also what makes the baseline race-free without leaning on that lock —
1120    /// exactly one caller can observe a prior watermark of zero, so exactly one stores.
1121    #[inline]
1122    pub fn note_committed(&self, index: SsaIndex, returned_packets: u64) {
1123        if self.committed_ssa_watermark.fetch_max(index.get(), Ordering::Relaxed) == 0 {
1124            self.returned_at_first_commit.store(returned_packets, Ordering::Relaxed);
1125        }
1126    }
1127
1128    /// Lowest index of the request last committed to, `None` before the first.
1129    #[inline]
1130    pub fn last_committed_first(&self) -> Option<SsaIndex> {
1131        SsaIndex::new(self.last_committed_first.load(Ordering::Relaxed))
1132    }
1133
1134    /// Records `index` as the lowest index of the request just committed to.
1135    ///
1136    /// A plain store: requests are serialised per pseudonym by the request lock, so there is no
1137    /// concurrent writer to order against, unlike the watermark's `fetch_max`.
1138    #[inline]
1139    pub fn note_committed_first(&self, index: SsaIndex) {
1140        self.last_committed_first.store(index.get(), Ordering::Relaxed);
1141    }
1142
1143    /// Records `members` as staged and not yet published, replacing whatever an older batch left.
1144    ///
1145    /// Called once phase two has staged the whole request and before phase three sends anything, so
1146    /// that a failure at any point of publication finds the whole batch still owed.
1147    pub fn stage_unpublished(&self, members: impl IntoIterator<Item = AgreedSsaQuota>) {
1148        let mut unpublished = self.unpublished.lock();
1149        unpublished.batch += 1;
1150        unpublished.members = members
1151            .into_iter()
1152            .map(|quota| (quota.ssa_id.ssa_index(), quota))
1153            .collect();
1154        unpublished.announced.clear();
1155        unpublished.last_sent = None;
1156    }
1157
1158    /// Takes the right to publish `index`, or `None` if nothing is owed for it or someone else holds it.
1159    ///
1160    /// The caller owns the announcement from here: it must either complete the publication or hand the
1161    /// member back through [`restore_unpublished`](Self::restore_unpublished).
1162    pub fn claim_unpublished(&self, index: SsaIndex) -> Option<ClaimedPublication> {
1163        let mut unpublished = self.unpublished.lock();
1164        let batch = unpublished.batch;
1165        unpublished
1166            .members
1167            .remove(&index)
1168            .map(|quota| ClaimedPublication { batch, quota })
1169    }
1170
1171    /// Hands back a claimed member whose publication did not complete, so that it is owed again.
1172    ///
1173    /// Dropped instead when a newer batch has been staged since the claim, which has replaced the one
1174    /// this member belonged to; there is nothing left for it to be owed to.
1175    pub fn restore_unpublished(&self, claim: ClaimedPublication) {
1176        let mut unpublished = self.unpublished.lock();
1177        if claim.batch == unpublished.batch {
1178            unpublished.members.insert(claim.quota.ssa_id.ssa_index(), claim.quota);
1179        }
1180    }
1181
1182    /// Spends a claim whose publication completed at `now`: the member's whole burst is out and its
1183    /// `ReadyToDeposit` queued.
1184    ///
1185    /// Recorded only while the claim's batch is the current one. A newer batch has replaced it
1186    /// otherwise, and the Exit no longer repeats the request this member belonged to.
1187    pub fn complete_publication(&self, claim: ClaimedPublication, now: Instant) {
1188        let mut unpublished = self.unpublished.lock();
1189        if claim.batch == unpublished.batch {
1190            unpublished.announced.insert(claim.quota.ssa_id.ssa_index());
1191            unpublished.last_sent = Some(now);
1192        }
1193    }
1194
1195    /// The announced members whose bursts a repeat arriving at `now` should have sent again, or
1196    /// nothing if the batch last went out less than `grace` ago.
1197    ///
1198    /// When it returns members, the batch counts as sent at `now`. The repeats that follow therefore
1199    /// wait out a whole `grace` again, and so do the ones that were already on their way. Whether
1200    /// the re-send then gets out does not matter: one that fails is retried no sooner than one that
1201    /// succeeded, which keeps a congested transport from being handed a burst on every repeat.
1202    pub fn claim_republication(&self, now: Instant, grace: Duration) -> Vec<SsaIndex> {
1203        let mut unpublished = self.unpublished.lock();
1204        let recently_sent = unpublished
1205            .last_sent
1206            .is_some_and(|sent| now.saturating_duration_since(sent) < grace);
1207        if recently_sent || unpublished.announced.is_empty() {
1208            return Vec::new();
1209        }
1210        unpublished.last_sent = Some(now);
1211        unpublished.announced.iter().copied().collect()
1212    }
1213
1214    /// Stops counting `index` as announced once the generator will not rebuild its burst, so later
1215    /// repeats do not ask for it again.
1216    pub fn forget_announced(&self, index: SsaIndex) {
1217        self.unpublished.lock().announced.remove(&index);
1218    }
1219
1220    /// Indices still owed a publication, ascending.
1221    pub fn unpublished_indices(&self) -> Vec<SsaIndex> {
1222        self.unpublished.lock().members.keys().copied().collect()
1223    }
1224
1225    /// Records a refusal, returning whether it differs from the one recorded before it.
1226    ///
1227    /// `first` is the lowest index the request asked for. A refusal repeated for the same index and
1228    /// the same reason returns `false`, so only its first occurrence is logged loudly.
1229    pub fn note_refusal(&self, first: Option<SsaIndex>, refusal: SsaRefusal) -> bool {
1230        let key = (u64::from(first.map_or(0, SsaIndex::get)) << 8) | refusal as u64;
1231        self.last_refusal.swap(key, Ordering::Relaxed) != key
1232    }
1233
1234    /// Exit → Entry packets received since this Session's first commitment.
1235    ///
1236    /// Saturating rather than wrapping: `returned_packets` is monotonic and the baseline is a past
1237    /// value of it, so an underflow is impossible — and if one ever became possible, reporting zero
1238    /// service closes the successor gate rather than opening it.
1239    #[inline]
1240    pub fn served_since_first_commit(&self, returned_packets: u64) -> u64 {
1241        returned_packets.saturating_sub(self.returned_at_first_commit.load(Ordering::Relaxed))
1242    }
1243
1244    /// Data quota one SSA cycle of these dimensions covers.
1245    ///
1246    /// The whole cycle, surplus included, as per [`pix_params_to_quota`]: every share a cycle emits
1247    /// rides one Exit → Entry packet, so all of them are priced.
1248    #[inline]
1249    pub const fn quota_per_ssa(&self) -> SsaQuota {
1250        pix_params_to_quota(&self.params)
1251    }
1252}
1253
1254/// The admission-token cell a [`SessionSlot`] shares with the [`SessionSlotGuard`] that allocated it.
1255///
1256/// Behind an `Arc` for two reasons. The slot is cloned into the sessions cache and into the guard, so
1257/// the token `commit` writes through the guard has to land in the *cached* copy every teardown reads
1258/// from — the `Arc` is that one shared cell. And it lets [`commit_slot_guard`] recognise its own slot
1259/// when it re-reads the cache by key: the key is a reusable pseudonym, so the entry found there may be
1260/// a successor Session's, and comparing this cell by identity is what rejects a foreign slot.
1261type AdmissionCell = Arc<OnceLock<AdmissionToken>>;
1262
1263#[derive(Clone)]
1264pub(crate) struct SessionSlot {
1265    // Sender does not need to be in Arc, because the receiver part is always
1266    // wrapped inside DropAbortable wrapper, with abort handle added to `abort_handles`.
1267    session_tx: crossfire::MTx<crossfire::mpsc::Array<ApplicationDataIn>>,
1268    routing_opts: DestinationRouting,
1269    // Additional tasks spawned by the Session.
1270    abort_handles: Arc<parking_lot::Mutex<AbortableList<SessionHandles>>>,
1271    // Allows reconfiguring of the SURB balancer on-the-fly
1272    // Set on both Entry and Exit sides.
1273    surb_mgmt: Arc<BalancerStateValues>,
1274    // SURB flow updates happening outside of Session protocol
1275    // (e.g., due to Start protocol messages).
1276    surb_estimator: AtomicSurbFlowEstimator,
1277    // Contains currently active SSA for this Session and its quota
1278    current_ssa_state: Arc<OnceLock<SessionSsaState>>,
1279    /// Handle to this Session's PIX supervisor, on the Exit side of a PIX-enabled Session.
1280    ///
1281    /// Populated before the [`HoprSession`] is constructed, so the egress adapters below observe a
1282    /// gate rather than racing its installation. Empty on the Entry side and on non-PIX Sessions —
1283    /// the Exit is authoritative for the lifecycle, so the Entry runs no supervisor.
1284    pix_supervisor: Arc<OnceLock<SessionPixSupervisorHandle>>,
1285    /// The egress gate every outgoing data packet of a supervised Session must pass.
1286    ///
1287    /// Held separately from `pix_supervisor` because the egress path touches it per packet and has
1288    /// no use for the rest of the handle.
1289    pix_egress_gate: Arc<OnceLock<Arc<ServiceGate>>>,
1290    /// Steers the Exit's own Exit → Entry keep-alive stream, where the Session has one.
1291    ///
1292    /// Exit-side, and populated for every PIX Session as well as for any Session with a configured
1293    /// `surb_balance_notify_period` — the two producers share one stream, so they share one handle.
1294    /// Empty on the Entry side, whose keep-alives are driven by its SURB balancer instead, and on an
1295    /// Exit Session that is neither PIX nor notifying, which originates nothing at all.
1296    ///
1297    /// A `OnceLock` for the same reason the two fields above are: the action driver that sets rates
1298    /// on it is spawned after the slot is published, so it must find the handle rather than race its
1299    /// installation.
1300    pix_fill: Arc<OnceLock<Arc<PixFillControl>>>,
1301    /// Exit → Entry Session packets received on this Session, ever.
1302    ///
1303    /// Entry-side only; stays zero on the Exit, which is the side that *sends* them. This includes
1304    /// both Session data and Start-protocol traffic such as the Exit's SURB-level keep-alives. Each
1305    /// packet consumed one return SURB, and a SURB carries at most one PIX share which the Exit can
1306    /// only decrypt by using it — so this counts shares the Exit has unlocked, measured without
1307    /// asking it. That is what makes it usable as a deposit gate: see the successor gate in
1308    /// [`SessionManager::handle_ssa_request`].
1309    ///
1310    /// Deliberately *not* [`surb_estimator`](Self::surb_estimator)`.consumed`, which increments on
1311    /// the same event on this side today. That field is documented as an *estimate* feeding the PID
1312    /// balancer, and it is only wired when `surb_management` is enabled; this one decides whether
1313    /// money is spent and must be neither. Carrying the increment twice is the cheaper mistake: a
1314    /// receive path that forgets this counter makes the gate stricter, never laxer.
1315    ///
1316    /// Credited from exactly two places, and both of them have to stay:
1317    ///
1318    /// * the `session_rx` inspectors in `new_session`, once per Session data packet handed to the reader — one in each
1319    ///   of the balanced and unbalanced branches;
1320    /// * the Start-protocol branch of [`dispatch_message`](SessionManager::dispatch_message), which credits every
1321    ///   Start-protocol message arriving on an outgoing Session because that traffic bypasses `session_rx` entirely.
1322    ///
1323    /// The second is what makes the Exit's keep-alives count, and the gate depends on it: an Exit
1324    /// whose application has nothing to say can still complete a funded cycle by keep-alive alone, and
1325    /// if those packets earned nothing here its successor would be refused as under-served and the
1326    /// Session would die on `CommitmentTimeout` with neither side able to name the cause. It is
1327    /// credited at the dispatch level rather than inside a per-message handler on purpose — the credit
1328    /// is owed for the SURB the packet consumed, which is true whatever the message turns out to be,
1329    /// including one this build fails to parse. Adding a second increment inside
1330    /// [`handle_keep_alive`](SessionManager::handle_keep_alive) would double-count it.
1331    returned_packets: Arc<std::sync::atomic::AtomicU64>,
1332    /// This Session's share of the node's live reconstructor-cycle budget.
1333    ///
1334    /// Exit-side and PIX-only; `None` everywhere else, since nothing else holds cycle state. Behind
1335    /// an `Arc` so the budget is returned when the last clone of this slot goes: a slot is cloned
1336    /// into the Session cache and into its [`SessionSlotGuard`], so no single one of them can be
1337    /// made responsible for the release.
1338    ///
1339    /// [`close_session`] returns it explicitly, which is what makes the release simultaneous with
1340    /// the closure; the `Drop` behind the `Arc` is the backstop for anything that bypasses that
1341    /// function. Both are safe to run because the release is idempotent.
1342    cycle_budget: Option<Arc<CycleBudgetReservation>>,
1343    /// The SURB-store admission this Session's `commit` obtains, threaded to the teardown so its
1344    /// retire can be matched to the admission it belongs to.
1345    ///
1346    /// Behind an `Arc` and empty until `commit` because the guard — which performs the `admit` — and
1347    /// the slot in the sessions cache are two clones of one value: the token has to land in the
1348    /// cached copy, and `commit` runs after the slot was inserted. Every teardown reads the token
1349    /// from the slot it removes, so it travels with the Session however long the teardown is delayed;
1350    /// empty stays [`AdmissionToken::NONE`], which matches no admission, so a rolled-back Session's
1351    /// retire is the no-op the seam's idempotency is there for.
1352    ///
1353    /// The same cell is what identifies this slot to the commit that allocated it — see
1354    /// [`AdmissionCell`].
1355    admission_token: AdmissionCell,
1356    /// The largest SURB target a `BalancerTarget` keep-alive has announced for this Session, or
1357    /// `None` while none has.
1358    ///
1359    /// Kept because the Exit answers `SessionEstablished` before it commits, so the Entry's ramp can
1360    /// announce a raised target in that window: the ring is sized at `commit`, from the target
1361    /// announced at establishment, and a raise that arrived earlier would otherwise be lost until the
1362    /// Entry announced it again. The commit applies this figure too, and every later raise widens the
1363    /// ring on the spot (see [`SurbAdmissionControl::raise_target`]).
1364    raised_surb_target: Arc<std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize>,
1365}
1366
1367impl SessionSlot {
1368    /// Claims the slot's admission-token cell on behalf of a teardown and returns what it holds.
1369    ///
1370    /// Empty means no `commit` has run yet, and the teardown claims the cell by storing
1371    /// [`AdmissionToken::NONE`] into it. That write is what lets a `commit` racing this teardown tell
1372    /// it lost: its own `set` then fails, and it retires the admission it just made instead of leaving
1373    /// a ring no teardown will ever remove. Without the claim, a teardown that read the empty cell
1374    /// would schedule a no-op retire, and a `commit` landing afterwards would admit a Session that is
1375    /// already gone — the leak the exit-side `SessionEstablished`-before-commit ordering makes
1376    /// reachable. Returns the token a later `commit` would have stored, or `NONE` when this teardown
1377    /// got there first (or the Session was never admitted at all).
1378    fn claim_admission_token(&self) -> AdmissionToken {
1379        *self.admission_token.get_or_init(|| AdmissionToken::NONE)
1380    }
1381
1382    /// The token this slot holds, or [`AdmissionToken::NONE`] while no `commit` has run.
1383    ///
1384    /// Read-only, unlike [`claim_admission_token`](Self::claim_admission_token): a keep-alive asking
1385    /// the store to widen this Session's ring must not *claim* the cell, or it would initialize it and
1386    /// make the establishment's own `commit` fail its `set` — retiring the live admission and leaving
